verdicts.why: A degree marker that scales whatever follows it; the attitude in 'so lost' or 'so subtle' belongs to the adjective, not to 'so'.
A pro-form standing in for a condition or manner already stated ('said so', 'thwarted so'); it points back without taking a side.
A connective marking consequence; it reports that one thing followed another and judges neither.
The plainest verb of speech, the neutral baseline that loaded neighbours like 'snap' or 'drawl' are measured against.
Utter aloud is a bare description of speaking; no attitude toward the speaker or the words rides on it.
'It has been said that' reports a claim without endorsing or doubting it, unlike 'allege' or 'insist'.
A pure intensifier; it strengthens 'sorry' or 'true' but adds no attitude of its own, and strength of meaning is not connotation.
'The very man' marks exact identity or emphasis of reference, a pointing function with no judgement in it.
'I see your design' names mental grasp plainly; the word does not approve or disparage what is grasped.
Perceiving by sight is the neutral core of the visual verbs; 'glimpse', 'gawk' and 'behold' are the loaded ones.
'See the less of him' means meet or spend time with, a plain statement of contact with no attitude attached.
Possessing a piece of information is stated flatly; the word neither praises the knower nor colours the fact.
Being acquainted with a person or thing is a relation, not a judgement of it.
Knowing how to do something reports competence without admiring or belittling it, unlike 'master' or 'dabble'.
'I thought him very sly' carries its judgement in 'sly'; 'think' merely frames the opinion as the speaker's own, without colouring it.
Believing or supposing is a plain hedge on certainty; 'presume' and 'fancy' are the neighbours with attitude.
Pondering or reasoning is the neutral verb of reflection; 'brood' and 'muse' are where the attitude lives.
'Make me happy', 'made her look handsomer' describes bringing about a state; the feeling is in the complement, not in 'make'.
'Made her a slight bow', 'make any reply' is a light verb carrying out an action, with no view of the action taken.
Causing someone to act is stated neutrally; 'force', 'coax' and 'bully' are the verbs that say how the causing lands.
The plainest verb of motion, against which 'trudge', 'flounce' and 'saunter' carry the attitude.
'Rose to go away' reports departure without the reproach of 'desert' or the relief of 'clear off'.
'Cannot go with the objectors', 'could not go on' names taking or continuing a course, a bare procedural fact.
A kinship term naming a relation; 'greatly superior to his sister' shows the judgement comes from elsewhere in the sentence.
Extending a kin word to a fellow member claims warmth and solidarity that the plain 'member' or 'colleague' does not; a learner should know it lands as affectionate belonging.
